newsitem.title: UK: London gold holds around $350, seeks new range.
newsitem.headline: London gold holds around $350, seeks new range.

text.p: Gold prices hovered around the psychological $350 an ounce level on Monday in what dealers called a bid to feel out a new price range.
The market was still skittish, however, after last week's news that the Swiss central bank planned to sell some of its gold reserves, dealers said.
Gold traded down to around $349.00 early on Monday, although physical demand helped push prices up slightly.
Bullion was fixed at $349.90 an ounce, compared with $350.30 on Friday afternoon and $348.80/$349.30 at the London close.
"Physical demand is probably going to keep gold around the $348-$350 area for now while it feels out a new range," a bullion dealer said.
Gold buyers in areas such as the Middle East, India and South East Asia were expected to be active at the lower prices, while gold producers were seen selling into any rallies.
But the big question in the near term was whether U.S.-based funds would decide to go short and drive down the price again, the dealer said.
"The funds squared up or at least are more neutral after the recent run-up to $364," he said.
Overshadowing the market was last week's news that Switzerland -- the world's most gold-friendly government -- was to sell part of its gold reserves to establish a Holocaust memorial fund.
Estimates went as high as 840 tonnes to be sold over 10 years, once the gold had been revalued.
"That suddenly puts the market under a lot more pressure," brokers GNI said in a commentary.
Silver was also off the boil, with technical indicators turning lower, analysts said.
At $5.15/$5.17, it was some four cents lower than on Friday and further slides were possible depending on gold and the other precious metals.
Platinum was off after investors in Asian markets took advantage of the widening spread between gold and platinum prices by buying gold while selling platinum.
It was at $377.50/$378.50, down $2.00 from Friday's London close.

Palladium, however, was barely changed at $148.25/$149.25 an ounce. The market was watching for fresh news of a threatened strike at Russia's Norilsk Nickel complex, a major world producer of the white metal, before testing the upside again.
